summary: For ages 9-10: count forwards and backwards in steps of powers of 10 (10; 100; 1,000; 10,000; 100,000) from any starting number up to 1,000,000, generalising earlier '10/100/1,000 more' work. The core insight is that each step changes exactly ONE place-value column — until a column fills and a roll-over (carry) cascades into the next column. Learners choose a step size and direction, track which digit ticks, and handle boundary crossings such as counting in 10,000s past 990,000 (reaching 1,000,000) or 492,000 up to 502,000. Work spans emerging (single power of 10, no boundary), secure (any power of 10 to 1,000,000, naming the changing digit), and extending (roll-over boundaries and predicting mixed sequences).
misconceptions: Changing the wrong column for the chosen step.
Boundary errors when a column rolls over (990,000 + 10,000).
Losing track of direction (counting back but incrementing).
Reverting to counting in ones for large steps.
Not generalising the pattern across different powers of 10.

activities.title: Single-column counting on a place-value chart
steps: Choose a step that is a power of ten (10; 100; 1,000; 10,000; or 100,000) and a direction (forwards or backwards).
Starting from a given number such as 462,000, count on in 10,000s aloud: 462,000 → 472,000 → 482,000 → 492,000, each time saying which single column changed.
On a place-value chart (e.g. a Gattegno chart) or with place-value counters, add or remove ONE counter in the chosen column per step and read the whole number.

Say the count structurally too, keeping the unchanged places fixed: '46 ten-thousands and 2 thousand, 47 ten-thousands and 2 thousand, 48 ten-thousands and 2 thousand...' so only the ten-thousands count ticks while the 2,000 stays put.
Repeat for a different power of ten (e.g. count back in 100,000s from 800,000: 700,000 → 600,000 → 500,000) and name the column that now ticks.
activities.insight: Counting in a power of ten means repeatedly nudging a SINGLE place-value column up or down while every other digit stays frozen, as long as no boundary is crossed; the chosen step decides which column ticks. (When a column rolls over, e.g. 492,000 → 502,000, a neighbouring column changes too. This is covered in the boundary activity.)

activities.title: Crossing the boundary: the roll-over cascade
steps: Count on in 10,000s and deliberately approach a boundary: 472,000 → 482,000 → 492,000 → 502,000, pausing at the crossing.
At 492,000, answer 'how many ten-thousands make the next hundred-thousand?' before stepping, then bridge to 502,000 and read the new hundred-thousands digit.
Count on in 10,000s up from 990,000 and watch the ten-thousands roll 9→0 while a carry cascades into the hundred-thousands and then the millions, reaching 1,000,000.

Count back in 10,000s across a boundary (522,000 → 512,000 → 502,000 → 492,000 → 482,000), noticing that at 502,000 → 492,000 the ten-thousands digit rolls back from 0 to 9 and the hundred-thousands digit decreases by one.
Predict a crossing before taking the step, then check: does only the next column change, or does the carry cascade further?
activities.insight: When a column fills, the single-column rule does not break — it cascades: counting forwards, the full column rolls over (9→0) and a carry moves into the next column, sometimes through several columns up to 1,000,000; counting backwards, an empty column rolls back (0→9) and the next column decreases by one.

activities.title: Spot the step and predict the next terms
steps: Look at an unlabelled sequence such as 375,000; 475,000; 575,000 and work out the step by comparing consecutive terms (here +100,000).
State the step as a power of ten and which column changes, then write or say the next three terms (675,000; 775,000; 875,000).
Try sequences that cross a boundary so a prediction requires a roll-over, e.g. continue counting on in 10,000s from 472,000 through 502,000.
Make and swap sequences with a partner: hide the upcoming terms and have them predict, then articulate the rule in words.
For a backwards sequence, confirm the terms decrease and name the changing column.
activities.insight: The counting pattern becomes reasoning: identifying a constant power-of-ten step lets you justify and predict any later term, including across boundaries.

checkQuestion: Count on out loud. (1) Start at 462,000 and count on in ten-thousands: 462,000... keep going for five more. (2) Start at 800,000 and count back in hundred-thousands. (3) A sequence goes 375,000; 475,000; 575,000 — what is the step, and what comes next?
